# API conventions (OSS + EE)

Scope: everything under `api/`. This file loads when you work in the API. The repo-wide
root conventions live in `/AGENTS.md`.

## Environment config conventions

- For API configuration, add new environment variables to `api/oss/src/utils/env.py` and
  consume them via the shared `env` object.
- Avoid calling `os.getenv(...)` directly in feature code when the value is part of
  application config.
- Avoid local imports inside helper functions for configuration lookup; prefer
  module-level imports unless there is a proven circular dependency.

## Formatting

Run `ruff format` then `ruff check --fix` within the API folder (from the repo root:
`ruff format` then `ruff check`). Fix all errors before committing.

## Code comments

Keep AI-generated in-code comments minimal. Comment only the non-obvious *why* (a subtle invariant, a workaround, a pool/concurrency hazard), never the *what* the code already states. Prefer one terse line over a multi-line block; do not narrate steps, restate the code, or leave TODO-style prose. If a comment is needed to explain *what* a block does, rename or extract instead.

## API Architecture Patterns

Use this section for all new work.

### API repo map

- `api/oss/src/*` is the OSS baseline API (new + legacy coexist here).
- `api/ee/src/*` is the EE extension API (billing, organizations, workspace, meters,
  subscriptions, throttling).
- `api/entrypoints/*` is the composition root (dependency wiring and route mounting).

OSS and EE relationship:
- OSS app is assembled first in `api/entrypoints/routers.py`.
- When `is_ee()` is true, EE extends that app via:
  - `ee.extend_main(app)` for extra routers/features.
  - `ee.extend_app_schema(app)` for OpenAPI/security metadata.
- EE is additive over OSS, not a separate API architecture.

RBAC / access enforcement:

- RBAC enforcement is an OSS feature and is always-on in both editions. The
  permission vocabulary, default role catalog, and enforcement service live in
  `api/oss/src/core/access/`. Handlers call `check_action_access(...)`
  unconditionally; there is no edition gate around the check itself.
- The only edition difference is the EE plan gate: in EE, `check_entitlements(Flag.RBAC)`
  can grant allow-all when a plan is not RBAC-entitled. This is layered into the OSS
  enforcement service via a function-local `is_ee()`-guarded import — OSS never imports
  `ee.*` at module top.
- Custom roles are an EE feature: `AGENTA_ACCESS_ROLES` / `AGENTA_ACCESS_ROLES_OVERLAY`
  are parsed/applied in `api/ee/src/core/access/permissions/role_overrides.py` and
  ignored in OSS (which enforces the code-default catalog).

Primary references:
- `api/entrypoints/routers.py`
- `api/ee/src/main.py`

### Where to add new API code

- Add new domain features in:
  - `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/<domain>/`
  - `api/oss/src/core/<domain>/`
  - `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/<domain>/`
- Avoid adding net-new features to legacy paths:
  - `api/oss/src/routers/*`
  - `api/oss/src/services/*`

### Standard domain folder structure

For a new domain, follow this shape:

- API layer: `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/<domain>/`
  - `router.py`: route registration + handlers
  - `models.py`: request/response schemas
  - `utils.py`: parsing/merge/normalization helpers
- Core layer: `api/oss/src/core/<domain>/`
  - `dtos.py` or `types.py`: domain data contracts
  - `interfaces.py`: DAO/service contracts when needed
  - `service.py`: business orchestration
- DB layer: `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/<domain>/`
  - `dbes.py`: SQLAlchemy entities
  - `dbas.py`: shared mixins (when needed)
  - `dao.py`: Postgres implementation
  - `mappings.py`: DTO <-> DBE mapping

Example to copy:
- `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/workflows/`
- `api/oss/src/core/workflows/`
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/workflows/`

### Database schema migrations (which alembic chain)

New tables/columns are alembic revisions. The legacy `core/` and `tracing/` chains are
**parked** (frozen at `park00000000`) — never add revisions there. Author against the
active chains:

- **Shared schema** (the default — runs in both OSS and EE): add the revision **once** in
  `oss/databases/postgres/migrations/core_oss/` (or `tracing_oss/`). EE ships and runs the
  `oss/` tree, so do **not** copy it into the EE tree.
- **EE-only schema** (genuinely edition-divergent): `ee/databases/postgres/migrations/core_ee/`
  (or `tracing_ee/`).

Full model (version tables, fresh-install/upgrade/OSS→EE-switch flows, FK and replay-skew
rules): `docs/designs/oss-ee-convergence/migration-chains-and-edition-switch.md`. For
alembic mechanics and docker commands, see the parked `core/README.md` — but always run
those commands from the appropriate active chain working directory (`core_oss`/`tracing_oss`
or `core_ee`/`tracing_ee`), not the parked `core/`/`tracing/` dirs.

### Layering and dependency direction

Required direction:
- Router -> Service -> DAO Interface -> DAO Implementation -> DB

Rules:
- Core services depend on interfaces (`*DAOInterface`), not concrete DB implementations.
- Wire concrete dependencies in `api/entrypoints/*` only.
- Keep DTO/DBE mapping in `dbs/postgres/*/mappings.py`.
- Do not return DBE objects from router/service contracts.
- As much as possible, define appropriate service exceptions (avoid leaking database
  exceptions).

### Endpoint design conventions

Use consistent endpoint shapes across domains:

- `POST /query` for filtering/search with payload support.
- `POST /{id}/archive` and `POST /{id}/unarchive` for lifecycle state transitions.
- For revisioned resources, expose:
  - `/revisions/retrieve`
  - `/revisions/commit`
  - `/revisions/log`

Request/response conventions:
- Define explicit request/response models in `models.py`.
- Response envelopes should include `count` plus payload (`item`/`items` style).
- Set explicit `operation_id` on routes.

Query conventions:
- Parse params via `Depends(...)` and optionally parse request body JSON.
- Merge params + body into one query object in `utils.py`.
- Use cursor pagination via `Windowing`, not page-number pagination.

References:
- `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/workflows/router.py`
- `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/workflows/utils.py`
- `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/shared/utils.py`
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/shared/utils.py`

### Git-style Artifact/Variant/Revision pattern

When a resource needs commit/history semantics, use the shared Git pattern instead of
inventing a custom one.

Use this pattern when you need:
- revision history and auditability
- latest vs specific revision retrieval
- revision logs
- variant forks/lineage

Core contracts:
- `api/oss/src/core/git/interfaces.py`
- `api/oss/src/core/git/dtos.py`

Postgres implementation:
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/git/dao.py`
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/git/dbas.py`

Domain DBE examples:
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/workflows/dbes.py`
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/queries/dbes.py`
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/testsets/dbes.py`

Service examples:
- `api/oss/src/core/workflows/service.py`
- `api/oss/src/core/queries/service.py`
- `api/oss/src/core/testsets/service.py`

Reuse pattern example:
- Evaluators reuse workflow persistence and can preserve IDs through
  `workflow_id=evaluator_id`.
- Reference: `api/oss/src/core/evaluators/service.py`

### Scope, lifecycle, and archival rules

- Always enforce tenant scope (`project_id` minimum) in DAO reads and writes.
- For revisioned entities, prefer archive/unarchive (`deleted_at`, `deleted_by_id`) over
  hard deletes.
- Respect `include_archived` in query paths.

References:
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/shared/dbas.py`
- `api/oss/src/dbs/postgres/git/dao.py`

### Migration and compatibility rules

Migration should preserve compatibility while moving to new APIs.

- Keep old and new routes running in parallel until migration is complete.
- New stack commonly ships under `/*` while old endpoints remain mounted.
- Prefer data compatibility adapters over breaking payload changes.
- Preserve old IDs/shape when continuity is required.
- If old storage temporarily carries new payload shape, mark it explicitly.

Concrete examples:
- Dual mounting and deprecations: `api/entrypoints/routers.py`
- Legacy app storage marker (`WORKFLOW_MARKER_KEY`):
  `api/oss/src/core/applications/service.py`
- Legacy dedup key normalization (`__dedup_id__` <-> `testcase_dedup_id`):
  `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/testsets/router.py`

### Router and function style conventions

Router style:
- Register routes inside router class `__init__` using `self.router.add_api_route(...)`.
- Use `@intercept_exceptions()` at the route boundary.
- Use `@suppress_exceptions(...)` only for controlled defaults.

Function signature style:
- Prefer keyword-only parameters using `*`.
- Use grouped sections in signatures/calls with `#` separators for readability.

Example:

```python
async def create_workflow(
    self,
    *,
    project_id: UUID,
    user_id: UUID,
    #
    workflow_create: WorkflowCreate,
    #
    workflow_id: Optional[UUID] = None,
) -> Optional[Workflow]:
    ...
```

### Domain-level exceptions

1. **Define domain exceptions in the core layer** (`core/{domain}/types.py` or
   `core/{domain}/dtos.py`) — never raise `HTTPException` from services or DAOs.
2. **Catch domain exceptions at the API boundary** — in the router or via a decorator —
   and convert them to HTTP responses.
3. **Use a base exception per domain** so callers can catch broadly or narrowly.
4. **Include structured context** (not just a message string) so the router can build
   rich HTTP error responses.

**Agent-actionable errors:** Expected domain failures exposed to an agent MUST use
`{code, message, retryable, next_step?, details?}`. `code` is a stable lower-snake-case
semantic cause; `message` is a concise diagnosis. `retryable` means the unchanged request
may safely succeed if repeated later. `retryable: true` requires one imperative
`next_step`; `next_step` may also accompany `retryable: false` when the caller must change
its request or state. Put every error-specific field in `details`; do not add other
top-level fields or nested `reason` envelopes. A code has one public HTTP status, but
handler-mode domain failures return HTTP 200 with `STATUS_CODE_ERROR` and the same
envelope in `ToolResult.content`. Core code raises typed exceptions; API and tool-handler
boundaries select the transport.

**Scope:** the envelope covers failures the PLATFORM authors. Third-party tool output
passes through as-is, symmetrically on success and failure, so a gateway tool's own failure
reason still reaches the model: that reason is what lets it correct a bad argument. On the
`/tools/call` seam this means every platform HANDLER emits the envelope, while the gateway
and workflow-tool arms carry their upstream's shape. Both arrive as errors. Do not read the
rule as "every `STATUS_CODE_ERROR` carries an envelope", and do not delete a consumer's
non-envelope path on that assumption.

The distinction that is easy to get wrong: `retryable` is about replaying the SAME request
unchanged, not about whether the caller has a way forward. A payload the caller must
correct is `retryable: false` WITH a `next_step`. Marking it retryable tells a small model
to send the identical bytes again, which cannot work and burns a turn.

**Example 1 — Folder exceptions (best example of the full pattern):**

Definition in `api/oss/src/core/folders/types.py`:
```python
class FolderNameInvalid(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str = "Folder name contains invalid characters."):
        self.message = message
        super().__init__(message)

class FolderPathConflict(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str = "A folder with this path already exists."):
        self.message = message
        super().__init__(message)
```

Raised in service `api/oss/src/core/folders/service.py`:
```python
def _validate_folder_name(name: Optional[str]) -> None:
    if not name or not fullmatch(r"[\w -]+", name):
        raise FolderNameInvalid()
```

Caught in router via decorator `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/folders/router.py`:
```python
def handle_folder_exceptions():
    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            try:
                return await func(*args, **kwargs)
            except FolderNameInvalid as e:
                raise FolderNameInvalidException(message=e.message) from e
            except FolderPathConflict as e:
                raise FolderPathConflictException(message=e.message) from e
        return wrapper
    return decorator
```

**Example 2 — Filtering exception (inline catch in router):**

Definition in `api/oss/src/core/tracing/dtos.py`:
```python
class FilteringException(Exception):
    pass
```

Caught in `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/tracing/router.py`:
```python
except FilteringException as e:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=str(e)) from e
```

**Example 3 — EE organization exceptions (base class hierarchy):**

Definition in `api/ee/src/core/organizations/exceptions.py`:
```python
class OrganizationError(Exception):
    """Base exception for organization-related errors."""
    pass

class OrganizationSlugConflictError(OrganizationError):
    def __init__(self, slug: str, message: str = None):
        self.slug = slug
        self.message = message or f"Organization slug '{slug}' is already in use."
        super().__init__(self.message)

class OrganizationNotFoundError(OrganizationError):
    def __init__(self, organization_id: str, message: str = None):
        self.organization_id = organization_id
        self.message = message or f"Organization '{organization_id}' not found."
        super().__init__(self.message)
```

Anti-patterns:
- Do NOT return error dicts like `{"_error": True, "status_code": 502, "detail": "..."}`
  from services or clients.
- Do NOT raise `HTTPException` from core services — that couples the domain to HTTP.
- Do NOT use bare `Exception` or `ValueError` for domain errors when a typed exception
  would be clearer.

### Typed DTO returns from services and clients

1. **Service methods must return typed DTOs** (Pydantic `BaseModel` subclasses), not raw
   dicts, tuples, or `Any`.
2. **HTTP clients should return a response DTO**, not
   `Tuple[Optional[Any], Optional[str]]`.
3. **Define DTOs in `core/{domain}/dtos.py`** alongside the domain's other data contracts.
4. **Use `Optional[DTO]` for missing entities**, `List[DTO]` for collections.

**Example — Workflow service returns typed DTOs:**

```python
# core/workflows/dtos.py
class Workflow(Artifact):
    pass

class WorkflowVariant(Variant):
    pass

# core/workflows/service.py
async def create_workflow(self, *, project_id, user_id, workflow_create) -> Optional[Workflow]:
    artifact = await self.workflows_dao.create_artifact(...)
    if not artifact:
        return None
    return Workflow(**artifact.model_dump(mode="json"))
```

**Example — HTTP client returns a DTO instead of a raw tuple:**

```python
# Instead of:
async def invoke(...) -> Tuple[Optional[Any], Optional[str]]:
    return data, trace_id  # untyped

# Do:
class InvokeResponse(BaseModel):
    data: Any
    trace_id: Optional[str] = None

async def invoke(...) -> InvokeResponse:
    return InvokeResponse(data=data, trace_id=trace_id)
```

Anti-patterns:
- Do NOT return raw dicts from service methods.
- Do NOT return tuples like `(data, trace_id)` — use a named DTO.
- Do NOT use `Dict[str, Any]` as a return type when you can define a proper model.

### Migration seams (do not copy for net-new code)

These exist during transition but should not be copied into new implementations:

- Core importing API routers/models directly
  - `api/oss/src/core/invocations/service.py`
  - `api/oss/src/core/annotations/service.py`
- Core importing legacy `db_manager` in new modules
  - `api/oss/src/core/workflows/service.py`
  - `api/oss/src/core/testsets/service.py`
  - `api/oss/src/core/evaluations/service.py`

Preferred fix for new work:
- introduce/extend core interfaces and adapters
- keep strict layer boundaries

</system-reminder>

1	---
2	name: spec-pages
3	description: Write an OpenSpec change for an Agenta feature, validate it, and publish two review pages for Mahmoud, a decision page with one card per open product question and an OpenSpec viewer with one tab per file. His answers update the spec. Use for every Feature and Program tier task in the build workflow, and when asked to "write the spec", "make the decision page", "render the OpenSpec", "spec review page", or "publish the spec for review".
4	---
5	
6	# Spec pages
7	
8	The OpenSpec change is the core artifact of a Feature or a Program. The design review, the
9	milestones, the implementation, the reviews and the QA all work from it. The `build` router
10	calls this skill for the Feature and Program tiers. Bug and Small change tiers do not use it.
11	
12	This skill makes three things:
13	
14	1. The OpenSpec change in `openspec/changes/<name>/`.
15	2. A decision page: one card per open product question, each with an example conversation,
16	   the options, and a recommendation.
17	3. An OpenSpec viewer: the change rendered exactly as written, one tab per file.
18	
19	Publish the decision page first, while product choices are open. Publish the viewer once the
20	spec is written and needs review.
21	
22	## Writing rules for both pages
23	
24	Load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and `~/.claude/skills/communicating-with-mahmoud/SKILL.md`
25	before you write. Then also follow these rules:
26	
27	- For every behavior, show today (from the code, with `file:line` in the spec) next to the
28	  expected behavior.
29	- Every choice lists its options, the trade-off of each option, and one recommendation with
30	  the reason.
31	- The decision page has no code talk. The OpenSpec files may name files, functions and
32	  config shapes.
33	- Keep the design small. Before you propose machinery for a rare case, ask whether a narrower
34	  rule or a documented limit is enough. The `review-simplify` lens explains how to judge it.
35	- When the change defines or changes an interface (API route, request or response field,
36	  wire field, config schema, tool definition, event payload), load the `design-interfaces`
37	  skill and classify each field by its role before the spec is final.
38	
39	## Step 1: Write the OpenSpec change
40	
41	Read the code first. Every "today" statement needs evidence. Create
42	`openspec/changes/<name>/` with these files:
43	
44	- `proposal.md`: `## Why`, `## What Changes`, `## Capabilities` (New and Modified), and
45	  `## Impact`.
46	- `design.md`: `## Context` (today's behavior, with evidence), `## Goals / Non-Goals`,
47	  `## Decisions` (each decision with a table of options and trade-offs, the chosen option in
48	  bold), then `## Risks / Trade-offs` and `## Migration`.
49	- `specs/<capability>/spec.md`: `## ADDED Requirements` (or `MODIFIED`). Under it,
50	  `### Requirement: <name>` with one sentence that uses SHALL, then one or more

---
name: spec-pages
description: Write an OpenSpec change for an Agenta feature, validate it, and publish two review pages for Mahmoud, a decision page with one card per open product question and an OpenSpec viewer with one tab per file. His answers update the spec. Use for every Feature and Program tier task in the build workflow, and when asked to "write the spec", "make the decision page", "render the OpenSpec", "spec review page", or "publish the spec for review".
---

# Spec pages

The OpenSpec change is the core artifact of a Feature or a Program. The design review, the
milestones, the implementation, the reviews and the QA all work from it. The `build` router
calls this skill for the Feature and Program tiers. Bug and Small change tiers do not use it.

This skill makes three things:

1. The OpenSpec change in `openspec/changes/<name>/`.
2. A decision page: one card per open product question, each with an example conversation,
   the options, and a recommendation.
3. An OpenSpec viewer: the change rendered exactly as written, one tab per file.

Publish the decision page first, while product choices are open. Publish the viewer once the
spec is written and needs review.

## Writing rules for both pages

Load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and `~/.claude/skills/communicating-with-mahmoud/SKILL.md`
before you write. Then also follow these rules:

- For every behavior, show today (from the code, with `file:line` in the spec) next to the
  expected behavior.
- Every choice lists its options, the trade-off of each option, and one recommendation with
  the reason.
- The decision page has no code talk. The OpenSpec files may name files, functions and
  config shapes.
- Keep the design small. Before you propose machinery for a rare case, ask whether a narrower
  rule or a documented limit is enough. The `review-simplify` lens explains how to judge it.
- When the change defines or changes an interface (API route, request or response field,
  wire field, config schema, tool definition, event payload), load the `design-interfaces`
  skill and classify each field by its role before the spec is final.

## Step 1: Write the OpenSpec change

Read the code first. Every "today" statement needs evidence. Create
`openspec/changes/<name>/` with these files:

- `proposal.md`: `## Why`, `## What Changes`, `## Capabilities` (New and Modified), and
  `## Impact`.
- `design.md`: `## Context` (today's behavior, with evidence), `## Goals / Non-Goals`,
  `## Decisions` (each decision with a table of options and trade-offs, the chosen option in
  bold), then `## Risks / Trade-offs` and `## Migration`.
- `specs/<capability>/spec.md`: `## ADDED Requirements` (or `MODIFIED`). Under it,
  `### Requirement: <name>` with one sentence that uses SHALL, then one or more
  `#### Scenario: <name>` blocks with `- **WHEN** ...` and `- **THEN** ...` lines.
- `tasks.md`: numbered sections with `- [ ] 1.1 ...` checkboxes. Mark tasks that can run in
  parallel. For a Program, group tasks by milestone; the `milestones` skill splits them.

Validate from the repo root:

```bash
npx @fission-ai/openspec validate <name> --strict
```

The command runs offline from the npx cache in about one second. With `--strict`, warnings
fail the check. The most common warning is a requirement body over 500 characters. Move
examples and edge cases into scenarios, or split the requirement.

## Step 2: Build the decision page

Copy `templates/decision-page.html` from this skill's folder and fill it in:

- `<title>`: a name of two to four words.
- `h1` and lede: what the feature is, and what the reader decides.
- Ability cards (optional): one per part of the feature.
- One `<section class="q">` per open question, with:
  - a numbered label (`Question 1`);
  - a question-style `h2`;
  - an example conversation in `.panel`: `.where` names the place, `.msg` rows are the
    person, `.msg.bot` rows are the agent's replies;
  - 2 to 4 `.opt` rows. Add `.spec` and the "in spec" badge to the option the written spec
    uses. Add `.rec` and the "recommended" badge to your recommendation;
  - one `.why` line.
- Footer: how to answer, by comments or with a line such as "1 recommended, 2 A".

Delete the instruction comment at the top before you publish.

## Step 3: Render the OpenSpec viewer

```bash
uv run ~/code/agenta/.claude/skills/spec-pages/scripts/render_openspec.py \
  <path/to/openspec/changes/<name>> "<Title, 2 to 4 words>" <out.html> "<source line, for example branch and SHA>"
```

The script embeds each Markdown file verbatim and renders it in the browser with `marked`
(pinned on cdnjs). The page has light and dark themes, sticky tabs, and tables that scroll
sideways, and it remembers the last open tab. Tab order: proposal, design, one tab per spec,
tasks, then any other Markdown file. It needs `uv` and Python 3.10 or later, and nothing
else. The output has a `<title>` but no doctype, `html`, `head` or `body` tags, because the
Artifact publisher wraps the page.

## Step 4: Publish and take answers

Write both pages in a run folder under `~/` (never `/tmp`), then publish each with the
Artifact tool. To update a page, write it to the same path and publish again; the URL stays
the same. Send Mahmoud a short note with both links and the questions he must answer.

When he answers:

1. Update the spec files to match each answer, and validate again.
2. On the decision page, add `decided` to the section class and change the label to
   `Question N, DECIDED: Option X`. Do not delete answered questions.
3. Re-render the viewer and publish both pages to the same URLs.

## Speed

- Read the code for different capabilities with several agents at once, and write the spec
  while they report.
- Publish the decision page as soon as the open questions are clear. Do not wait for the full
  spec before you ask.
- Validate and render with the commands above. Each takes seconds, so run them after every
  change instead of batching.
- Start the design review (`review-loop` in design mode) on the parts of the spec that the
  open questions do not touch.

1	---
2	name: plain-writing
3	description: >-
4	  Writes and edits prose in a plain and boring style: simple everyday words,
5	  complete sentences, no dashes, no jargon, and no analogies. Use when
6	  drafting or revising documents, Notion pages, reports, summaries, READMEs,
7	  emails, slides, commit messages, or PR descriptions, or when the user asks
8	  to simplify, clean up, tighten, reword, or make writing clearer. Use when
9	  the user invokes /plain-writing deslopify or asks to deslopify an agent
10	  response. Do not apply to code, only to the words around it.
11	license: MIT
12	---
13	
14	# Plain writing
15	
16	The plain writing skill captures how the user wants writing to read: plain,
17	boring, and easy to understand in one pass. Apply it by default when you write
18	for them.
19	
20	There are four groups of rules: word choice and tone, sentences and paragraphs,
21	punctuation and formatting, and patterns to avoid. Each rule has a before and
22	after. After the rules comes the deslopify command.
23	
24	## Word choice and tone
25	
26	1. **Use simple, everyday words.** Don't pick a fancy synonym when a plain word
27	   works. Also avoid words AI tools overuse, e.g., "delve", "tapestry",
28	   "landscape", "robust", "leverage", and "reach".
29	   Before: We leverage the cache to unlock a more robust query experience.
30	   After: We use the cache to make repeated queries faster.
31	
32	2. **No jargon.** Always use human-understandable language, the way two people
33	   talk to each other. Don't invent jargon or shorthand (that is, if a word or
34	   phrase is not in the Merriam Webster dictionary, don't use it). Use
35	   established technical terms only when they are most precise, and briefly
36	   define them when readers may not know them.
37	   Before: The score is a calibrated proxy for whether the property holds.
38	   After: The score estimates how likely the property is to hold.
39	
40	3. **No puffery or empty emphasis.** Drop words that add emphasis but no
41	   information, e.g., "really", "real", "matters", "worth", "carries weight",
42	   "boasts", "a testament to", "pivotal", "renowned", and "quietly". State the
43	   actual point, or cut the sentence.
44	   Before: This result matters, and it carries weight for the design.
45	   After: The scores barely moved, so we can skip the model on most documents.
46	
47	4. **Use consistent terminology and constrain your vocabulary.**
48	   Before: Upload the document. The file is parsed, and the record is saved.
49	   After: Upload the document. The document is parsed and saved.
50	
51	5. **It's ok to use contractions.** They match everyday speech, so use them
52	   freely.
53	   Before: Do not worry, it is not going to overwrite your file.
54	   After: Don't worry, it's not going to overwrite your file.
55	
56	6. **Do not invent hyphenated adjectives.** Avoid a phrase you make up by
57	   joining words with a hyphen to sound compact or clever. If you would not find
58	   it in a dictionary, don't use it. A common compound adjective that people
59	   already use is fine, e.g., "well-crafted".
60	   Before: We added a reveal-style colon to the output.
61	   After: We added a colon that shows the schema.
62	
63	7. **Keep the writing boring, descriptive, and explanatory.** Do not use a
64	   catchy phrase, slogan, clever label, or wording meant to sound memorable.
65	   This rule applies everywhere; to headings, topic sentences, callouts,
66	   labels, summaries, and ordinary prose.
67	   Before: Legal requirements as a floor.
68	   After: Applicable legal constraints.
69	   Before: # The alignment loop
70	   After: # Iterative refinement using development disagreements
71	
72	## Sentences and paragraphs
73	
74	8. **Write complete sentences.** Each sentence should have a subject and a
75	   verb. Do not write fragments, and do not stitch unrelated ideas together with
76	   colons or semicolons. But it is ok to join closely related ideas with plain
77	   conjunctions, like "and", "because", or "so".
78	   Before: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes, and the team meets on
79	   Tuesdays.
80	   After: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes. The team meets on
81	   Tuesdays.
82	
83	9. **When you present a workflow or sequence, walk through it in order.** Use
84	   "First", "Second", "Third", and give each step its own sentence so the
85	   reader can follow it, or break up steps with semicolons.
86	   Before: The groups the features were sorted into were the authors' own
87	   reading, the example posts were written by hand, and finer detail meant
88	   training extra small models and labeling again.
89	   After: First, the authors sorted the features into groups themselves, based on
90	   their own reading of the outputs. Second, they wrote the example posts by
91	   hand. Third, when they wanted finer detail, they trained another small
92	   model, and they labeled the posts again.
93	
94	10. **Organize a paragraph as a topic sentence and then support.** Start each
95	   paragraph or section with a topic sentence that states the main point. Then,
96	   the next sentence should be a supporting example or fact, with an extra
97	   sentence about it if it needs one. Then, introduce more support with a plain
98	   connective like "For example", "Moreover", or "Or".
99	   Before: The parser skips files with no changes. The cache holds the previous
100	   output. Most renders are fast.
101	   After: Most renders are fast. For example, the parser skips files with no
102	   changes, so the server returns early. Moreover, the cache keeps the previous
103	   output, so a repeated render does no work.
104	
105	11. **Never write three or more clauses in one sentence, or three or more
106	    example sentences in a row.** In ordinary prose, a sentence may have one or
107	    two related clauses. Do not pack three or more clauses into one prose
108	    sentence. If you need that many points, use a numbered First / Second / Third
109	    sequence under rule 9, or short bullet points when you are writing a
110	    brief. If list points are examples and you want to inline them, introduce
111	    with "e.g.". Also do not give three or more example sentences back to back
112	    to support the same point.
113	    Before: The parser reads the file, the validator checks the fields, and the
114	    writer saves the record.
115	    After: The parser reads the file, and the validator checks the fields. The
116	    writer then saves the record.
117	
118	12. **Prefer long, explanatory sentences over short, punchy ones.** In ordinary
119	    prose, write the way people explain things out loud: longer sentences with
120	    commas, and the simplest way to say the point. Do not break one thought into
121	    a stack of short sentences, and don't write catchy short phrases. Short
122	    lines are fine only in labeled briefs, bullets, or a First / Second / Third
123	    sequence, e.g., "To do: validate recall on long queries."
124	    Before: The gate runs on every merge. It blocks regressions. Nobody
125	    bypasses it.
126	    After: The gate runs on every merge, and it blocks changes that fail a
127	    regression case. A regression cannot make it to production, unless someone
128	    deliberately overrides the check.
129	    Before: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics. The
130	    change reduced p95 latency from 900 ms to 220 ms. We still need to validate
131	    recall on long queries.
132	    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics, and
133	    p95 latency fell from 900 ms to 220 ms. To do: validate recall on long
134	    queries.
135	
136	13. **Be precise and unambiguous, and cut unnecessary clauses.** Say exactly
137	    what changes, who does what, or by what mechanism. Prefer a concrete
138	    statement over an evocative abstraction, e.g., don't say things like
139	    "improvement stops being guesswork". Also drop trailing or side clauses
140	    that add no fact, e.g., "before we call the work done", "as we move
141	    forward", or "for the time being". Keep the sentence long when the content
142	    needs it, but do not pad it.
143	    Before: With trusted scores, improvement stops being guesswork.
144	    After: With trusted scores, you can measure whether each change helped,
145	    so you keep or revert each change based on the measured result.
146	    Before: We still need to validate recall on long queries before we call
147	    the work done.
148	    After: To do: validate recall on long queries.
149	
150	14. **In chat, give context on the problem.** When you are chatting back and
151	    forth, write for a smart reader who does not have context on the problem,
152	    or who forgot it. Give context on the problem and on what was happening
153	    before. Then say what changed. Keep the setup short. Do not dump the whole
154	    history. Ignore this rule if you are writing an essay.
155	    Before: The exporter now waits on the reset header, and `dotnet test` is
156	    green.
157	    After: The Okta System Log exporter was rereading whole hours, so a retry
158	    could write the same event twice. It now waits using the response reset
159	    header, and the six acceptance tests pass.
160	
161	## Punctuation and formatting
162	
163	15. **No dashes or middle dots.** Do not use em dashes or en dashes, including in
164	    number ranges. Join clauses with a period or "and", and write ranges with
165	    "to". Do not use the middle dot (·) as a separator; use a comma, "and", or
166	    separate lines instead.
167	    Before: The build is fast — it finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
168	    After: The build is fast. It finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
169	
170	16. **Don't use colons to join clauses in ordinary prose.** Do not use a colon
171	    to glue two clauses or to set up a point in essay-like writing. A colon is
172	    fine when you introduce a list. A colon is also fine as a short label in
173	    updates, briefs, status notes, and PR descriptions, e.g., "Summary:",
174	    "Changes:", or "Remaining work:".
175	    Before: Read for the schema: the feature fires.
176	    After: Read for the schema. The feature fires.
177	    Before (allowed in a PR or update): Summary: Replace em dashes in
178	    generated docs.
179	    After (same text is fine): Summary: Replace em dashes in generated docs.
180	
181	17. **Use straight quotes, not curly quotes.**
182	    Before: The system logs each “event” as it happens.
183	    After: The system logs each "event" as it happens.
184	
185	18. **Keep the formatting plain.** Use sentence case in headings. Do not use
186	    bold for decoration.
187	    Before: ## How To Install The Skill
188	    After: ## How to install the skill
189	
190	19. **You can use lists, but do not overuse them.** Keep a list to three or
191	    four points, and nest extra points if you need more. When you are writing
192	    an essay, use lists and tables very sparingly.
193	    Before: Shipped this week:
194	    - dark mode
195	    - an invite link fix
196	    - a schema mismatch that blocked analytics export
197	    - renderer cleanup
198	    - copy edits
199	    - a scored ranking model
200	    - a p95 drop from 900 ms to 220 ms
201	    - untested recall on long queries
202	    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model, and p95 latency fell from
203	    900 ms to 220 ms. The old heuristic path is still in the repo as a
204	    fallback.
205	    - Shipped
206	      - Dark mode
207	      - Invite link fix
208	    - Still open
209	      - Test recall on long queries
210	      - Unblock analytics export
211	
212	## Patterns to avoid
213	
214	20. **Do not give inanimate things fake agency.** Do not write as if a system
215	    or object transforms, decides, or intends on its own when a person or
216	    process is the real actor. Ordinary factual verbs for tools and systems are
217	    fine, e.g., "The API returns JSON", "The job writes the file", or "The
218	    paper argues". Prefer a human or process subject when that is clearer.
219	    Before: The logs become searchable records, once the job finishes.
220	    After: You can search the logs, once the job finishes.
221	
222	21. **No analogies or imagery.** Do not explain by comparing to something else,
223	    and do not use metaphor. Describe the actual thing in literal terms. Write
224	    in a boring way.
225	    Before: The feature index is like a card catalog that the optimizer can flip
226	    through.
227	    After: The feature index is a list of named features. The optimizer can look
228	    up which feature matches a request.
229	
230	22. **Never use negative parallelism of the form "not just X, it is Y" or
231	    "not only X, but Y".** State what the thing is. A plain refusal or
232	    correction is fine, including a short quote of a customer's hype phrase
233	    when you replace it with a concrete fact.
234	    Before: It is not just a parser, it is a full toolchain.
235	    After: It is a parser and a formatter.
236	    Before: We do not describe the API as "enterprise-grade robust," because
237	    that phrase can mean different things.
238	    After: The API has a 99.9% monthly uptime SLO.
239	
240	23. **Do not stack rhetorical questions.** AI writing often asks two or three
241	    rhetorical questions in a row to sound thoughtful. Don't do this. Just state
242	    the problem directly.
243	    Before: Does the tool keep the writer's voice? Does it make the argument
244	    stronger or weaker?
245	    After: We do not yet know whether the tool keeps the writer's voice, or
246	    whether it makes the argument stronger or weaker.
247	
248	24. **Do not use vague demonstrative pronouns.** Do not use "This", "That",
249	    "These", or "Those", especially do not start a sentence with a demonstrative
250	    pronoun, and never begin a paragraph with a sentence that contains a
251	    demonstrative anywhere in it.
252	    Before: That context carries into the next turn.
253	    After: The agent applies the rules you saved on the next turn.
254	
255	25. **Do not open with a count of things.** Never start by announcing how many
256	    points are coming, e.g., "Two cautions." or "Three things to keep in mind."
257	    State the first point directly. If you absolutely must present many things,
258	    use a bullet list instead.
259	    Before: Two cautions. First, the section can drift out of date. Second,
260	    it can balloon if every item gets a sentence.
261	    After: The section can drift out of date, because it duplicates facts
262	    that live elsewhere. It can also balloon if every item gets a sentence.
263	
264	## The deslopify command
265	
266	When the user says `/plain-writing deslopify`, rewrite the previous agent
267	response, or the text after the command, for a sharp CEO or technical reader
268	who has no project context. Return only the rewrite.
269	
270	Start with the main conclusion, then cover the background, how it works, and
271	present all information logically and sequentially. Include technical details
272	the reader needs (standardize on existing well-known terminology, not new
273	terminology), and define unfamiliar terms.
274	
275	Follow the plain-writing rules above.
276

   it in a dictionary, don't use it. A common compound adjective that people
   already use is fine, e.g., "well-crafted".
   Before: We added a reveal-style colon to the output.
   After: We added a colon that shows the schema.

7. **Keep the writing boring, descriptive, and explanatory.** Do not use a
   catchy phrase, slogan, clever label, or wording meant to sound memorable.
   This rule applies everywhere; to headings, topic sentences, callouts,
   labels, summaries, and ordinary prose.
   Before: Legal requirements as a floor.
   After: Applicable legal constraints.
   Before: # The alignment loop
   After: # Iterative refinement using development disagreements

## Sentences and paragraphs

8. **Write complete sentences.** Each sentence should have a subject and a
   verb. Do not write fragments, and do not stitch unrelated ideas together with
   colons or semicolons. But it is ok to join closely related ideas with plain
   conjunctions, like "and", "because", or "so".
   Before: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes, and the team meets on
   Tuesdays.
   After: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes. The team meets on
   Tuesdays.

9. **When you present a workflow or sequence, walk through it in order.** Use
   "First", "Second", "Third", and give each step its own sentence so the
   reader can follow it, or break up steps with semicolons.
   Before: The groups the features were sorted into were the authors' own
   reading, the example posts were written by hand, and finer detail meant
   training extra small models and labeling again.
   After: First, the authors sorted the features into groups themselves, based on
   their own reading of the outputs. Second, they wrote the example posts by
   hand. Third, when they wanted finer detail, they trained another small
   model, and they labeled the posts again.

10. **Organize a paragraph as a topic sentence and then support.** Start each
   paragraph or section with a topic sentence that states the main point. Then,
   the next sentence should be a supporting example or fact, with an extra
   sentence about it if it needs one. Then, introduce more support with a plain
   connective like "For example", "Moreover", or "Or".
   Before: The parser skips files with no changes. The cache holds the previous
   output. Most renders are fast.
   After: Most renders are fast. For example, the parser skips files with no
   changes, so the server returns early. Moreover, the cache keeps the previous
   output, so a repeated render does no work.

11. **Never write three or more clauses in one sentence, or three or more
    example sentences in a row.** In ordinary prose, a sentence may have one or
    two related clauses. Do not pack three or more clauses into one prose
    sentence. If you need that many points, use a numbered First / Second / Third
    sequence under rule 9, or short bullet points when you are writing a
    brief. If list points are examples and you want to inline them, introduce
    with "e.g.". Also do not give three or more example sentences back to back
    to support the same point.
    Before: The parser reads the file, the validator checks the fields, and the
    writer saves the record.
    After: The parser reads the file, and the validator checks the fields. The
    writer then saves the record.

12. **Prefer long, explanatory sentences over short, punchy ones.** In ordinary
    prose, write the way people explain things out loud: longer sentences with
    commas, and the simplest way to say the point. Do not break one thought into
    a stack of short sentences, and don't write catchy short phrases. Short
    lines are fine only in labeled briefs, bullets, or a First / Second / Third
    sequence, e.g., "To do: validate recall on long queries."
    Before: The gate runs on every merge. It blocks regressions. Nobody
    bypasses it.
    After: The gate runs on every merge, and it blocks changes that fail a
    regression case. A regression cannot make it to production, unless someone
    deliberately overrides the check.
    Before: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics. The
    change reduced p95 latency from 900 ms to 220 ms. We still need to validate
    recall on long queries.
    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics, and
    p95 latency fell from 900 ms to 220 ms. To do: validate recall on long
    queries.

13. **Be precise and unambiguous, and cut unnecessary clauses.** Say exactly
    what changes, who does what, or by what mechanism. Prefer a concrete
    statement over an evocative abstraction, e.g., don't say things like
    "improvement stops being guesswork". Also drop trailing or side clauses
    that add no fact, e.g., "before we call the work done", "as we move
    forward", or "for the time being". Keep the sentence long when the content
    needs it, but do not pad it.
    Before: With trusted scores, improvement stops being guesswork.
    After: With trusted scores, you can measure whether each change helped,
    so you keep or revert each change based on the measured result.
    Before: We still need to validate recall on long queries before we call
    the work done.
    After: To do: validate recall on long queries.

14. **In chat, give context on the problem.** When you are chatting back and
    forth, write for a smart reader who does not have context on the problem,
    or who forgot it. Give context on the problem and on what was happening
    before. Then say what changed. Keep the setup short. Do not dump the whole
    history. Ignore this rule if you are writing an essay.
    Before: The exporter now waits on the reset header, and `dotnet test` is
    green.
    After: The Okta System Log exporter was rereading whole hours, so a retry
    could write the same event twice. It now waits using the response reset
    header, and the six acceptance tests pass.

## Punctuation and formatting

15. **No dashes or middle dots.** Do not use em dashes or en dashes, including in
    number ranges. Join clauses with a period or "and", and write ranges with
    "to". Do not use the middle dot (·) as a separator; use a comma, "and", or
    separate lines instead.
    Before: The build is fast — it finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
    After: The build is fast. It finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.

16. **Don't use colons to join clauses in ordinary prose.** Do not use a colon
    to glue two clauses or to set up a point in essay-like writing. A colon is
    fine when you introduce a list. A colon is also fine as a short label in
    updates, briefs, status notes, and PR descriptions, e.g., "Summary:",
    "Changes:", or "Remaining work:".
    Before: Read for the schema: the feature fires.
    After: Read for the schema. The feature fires.
    Before (allowed in a PR or update): Summary: Replace em dashes in
    generated docs.
    After (same text is fine): Summary: Replace em dashes in generated docs.

17. **Use straight quotes, not curly quotes.**
    Before: The system logs each “event” as it happens.
    After: The system logs each "event" as it happens.

18. **Keep the formatting plain.** Use sentence case in headings. Do not use
    bold for decoration.
    Before: ## How To Install The Skill
    After: ## How to install the skill

19. **You can use lists, but do not overuse them.** Keep a list to three or
    four points, and nest extra points if you need more. When you are writing
    an essay, use lists and tables very sparingly.
    Before: Shipped this week:
    - dark mode
    - an invite link fix
    - a schema mismatch that blocked analytics export
    - renderer cleanup
    - copy edits
    - a scored ranking model
    - a p95 drop from 900 ms to 220 ms
    - untested recall on long queries
    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model, and p95 latency fell from
    900 ms to 220 ms. The old heuristic path is still in the repo as a
    fallback.
    - Shipped
      - Dark mode
      - Invite link fix
    - Still open
      - Test recall on long queries
      - Unblock analytics export

## Patterns to avoid

20. **Do not give inanimate things fake agency.** Do not write as if a system
    or object transforms, decides, or intends on its own when a person or
    process is the real actor. Ordinary factual verbs for tools and systems are
    fine, e.g., "The API returns JSON", "The job writes the file", or "The
    paper argues". Prefer a human or process subject when that is clearer.
    Before: The logs become searchable records, once the job finishes.
    After: You can search the logs, once the job finishes.

21. **No analogies or imagery.** Do not explain by comparing to something else,
    and do not use metaphor. Describe the actual thing in literal terms. Write
    in a boring way.
    Before: The feature index is like a card catalog that the optimizer can flip
    through.
    After: The feature index is a list of named features. The optimizer can look
    up which feature matches a request.

22. **Never use negative parallelism of the form "not just X, it is Y" or
    "not only X, but Y".** State what the thing is. A plain refusal or
    correction is fine, including a short quote of a customer's hype phrase
    when you replace it with a concrete fact.
    Before: It is not just a parser, it is a full toolchain.
    After: It is a parser and a formatter.
    Before: We do not describe the API as "enterprise-grade robust," because
    that phrase can mean different things.
    After: The API has a 99.9% monthly uptime SLO.

23. **Do not stack rhetorical questions.** AI writing often asks two or three
    rhetorical questions in a row to sound thoughtful. Don't do this. Just state
    the problem directly.
    Before: Does the tool keep the writer's voice? Does it make the argument
    stronger or weaker?
    After: We do not yet know whether the tool keeps the writer's voice, or
    whether it makes the argument stronger or weaker.

24. **Do not use vague demonstrative pronouns.** Do not use "This", "That",
    "These", or "Those", especially do not start a sentence with a demonstrative
    pronoun, and never begin a paragraph with a sentence that contains a
    demonstrative anywhere in it.
    Before: That context carries into the next turn.
    After: The agent applies the rules you saved on the next turn.

25. **Do not open with a count of things.** Never start by announcing how many
    points are coming, e.g., "Two cautions." or "Three things to keep in mind."
    State the first point directly. If you absolutely must present many things,
    use a bullet list instead.
    Before: Two cautions. First, the section can drift out of date. Second,
    it can balloon if every item gets a sentence.
    After: The section can drift out of date, because it duplicates facts
    that live elsewhere. It can also balloon if every item gets a sentence.

## The deslopify command

When the user says `/plain-writing deslopify`, rewrite the previous agent
response, or the text after the command, for a sharp CEO or technical reader
who has no project context. Return only the rewrite.

Start with the main conclusion, then cover the background, how it works, and
present all information logically and sequentially. Include technical details
the reader needs (standardize on existing well-known terminology, not new
terminology), and define unfamiliar terms.

Follow the plain-writing rules above.

1	---
2	name: spec-pages
3	description: Write an OpenSpec change for an Agenta feature, validate it, and publish two review pages for Mahmoud, a decision page with one card per open product question and an OpenSpec viewer with one tab per file. His answers update the spec. Use for every Feature and Program tier task in the build workflow, and when asked to "write the spec", "make the decision page", "render the OpenSpec", "spec review page", or "publish the spec for review".
4	---
5	
6	# Spec pages
7	
8	The OpenSpec change is the core artifact of a Feature or a Program. The design review, the
9	milestones, the implementation, the reviews and the QA all work from it. The `build` router
10	calls this skill for the Feature and Program tiers. Bug and Small change tiers do not use it.
11	
12	This skill makes three things:
13	
14	1. The OpenSpec change in `openspec/changes/<name>/`.
15	2. A decision page: one card per open product question, each with an example conversation,
16	   the options, and a recommendation.
17	3. An OpenSpec viewer: the change rendered exactly as written, one tab per file.
18	
19	Publish the decision page first, while product choices are open. Publish the viewer once the
20	spec is written and needs review.
21	
22	## Writing rules for both pages
23	
24	Load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and `~/.claude/skills/communicating-with-mahmoud/SKILL.md`
25	before you write. Then also follow these rules:
26	
27	- For every behavior, show today (from the code, with `file:line` in the spec) next to the
28	  expected behavior.
29	- Every choice lists its options, the trade-off of each option, and one recommendation with
30	  the reason.
31	- The decision page has no code talk. The OpenSpec files may name files, functions and
32	  config shapes.
33	- Keep the design small. Before you propose machinery for a rare case, ask whether a narrower
34	  rule or a documented limit is enough. The `review-simplify` lens explains how to judge it.
35	- When the change defines or changes an interface (API route, request or response field,
36	  wire field, config schema, tool definition, event payload), load the `design-interfaces`
37	  skill and classify each field by its role before the spec is final.
38	
39	## Step 1: Write the OpenSpec change
40	
41	Read the code first. Every "today" statement needs evidence. Create
42	`openspec/changes/<name>/` with these files:
43	
44	- `proposal.md`: `## Why`, `## What Changes`, `## Capabilities` (New and Modified), and
45	  `## Impact`.
46	- `design.md`: `## Context` (today's behavior, with evidence), `## Goals / Non-Goals`,
47	  `## Decisions` (each decision with a table of options and trade-offs, the chosen option in
48	  bold), then `## Risks / Trade-offs` and `## Migration`.
49	- `specs/<capability>/spec.md`: `## ADDED Requirements` (or `MODIFIED`). Under it,
50	  `### Requirement: <name>` with one sentence that uses SHALL, then one or more
51	  `#### Scenario: <name>` blocks with `- **WHEN** ...` and `- **THEN** ...` lines.
52	- `tasks.md`: numbered sections with `- [ ] 1.1 ...` checkboxes. Mark tasks that can run in
53	  parallel. For a Program, group tasks by milestone; the `milestones` skill splits them.
54	
55	Validate from the repo root:
56	
57	```bash
58	npx @fission-ai/openspec validate <name> --strict
59	```
60	
61	The command runs offline from the npx cache in about one second. With `--strict`, warnings
62	fail the check. The most common warning is a requirement body over 500 characters. Move
63	examples and edge cases into scenarios, or split the requirement.
64	
65	## Step 2: Build the decision page
66	
67	Copy `templates/decision-page.html` from this skill's folder and fill it in:
68	
69	- `<title>`: a name of two to four words.
70	- `h1` and lede: what the feature is, and what the reader decides.
71	- Ability cards (optional): one per part of the feature.
72	- One `<section class="q">` per open question, with:
73	  - a numbered label (`Question 1`);
74	  - a question-style `h2`;
75	  - an example conversation in `.panel`: `.where` names the place, `.msg` rows are the
76	    person, `.msg.bot` rows are the agent's replies;
77	  - 2 to 4 `.opt` rows. Add `.spec` and the "in spec" badge to the option the written spec
78	    uses. Add `.rec` and the "recommended" badge to your recommendation;

1	---
2	name: plain-writing
3	description: >-
4	  Writes and edits prose in a plain and boring style: simple everyday words,
5	  complete sentences, no dashes, no jargon, and no analogies. Use when
6	  drafting or revising documents, Notion pages, reports, summaries, READMEs,
7	  emails, slides, commit messages, or PR descriptions, or when the user asks
8	  to simplify, clean up, tighten, reword, or make writing clearer. Use when
9	  the user invokes /plain-writing deslopify or asks to deslopify an agent
10	  response. Do not apply to code, only to the words around it.
11	license: MIT
12	---
13	
14	# Plain writing
15	
16	The plain writing skill captures how the user wants writing to read: plain,
17	boring, and easy to understand in one pass. Apply it by default when you write
18	for them.
19	
20	There are four groups of rules: word choice and tone, sentences and paragraphs,
21	punctuation and formatting, and patterns to avoid. Each rule has a before and
22	after. After the rules comes the deslopify command.
23	
24	## Word choice and tone
25	
26	1. **Use simple, everyday words.** Don't pick a fancy synonym when a plain word
27	   works. Also avoid words AI tools overuse, e.g., "delve", "tapestry",
28	   "landscape", "robust", "leverage", and "reach".
29	   Before: We leverage the cache to unlock a more robust query experience.
30	   After: We use the cache to make repeated queries faster.
31	
32	2. **No jargon.** Always use human-understandable language, the way two people
33	   talk to each other. Don't invent jargon or shorthand (that is, if a word or
34	   phrase is not in the Merriam Webster dictionary, don't use it). Use
35	   established technical terms only when they are most precise, and briefly
36	   define them when readers may not know them.
37	   Before: The score is a calibrated proxy for whether the property holds.
38	   After: The score estimates how likely the property is to hold.
39	
40	3. **No puffery or empty emphasis.** Drop words that add emphasis but no
41	   information, e.g., "really", "real", "matters", "worth", "carries weight",
42	   "boasts", "a testament to", "pivotal", "renowned", and "quietly". State the
43	   actual point, or cut the sentence.
44	   Before: This result matters, and it carries weight for the design.
45	   After: The scores barely moved, so we can skip the model on most documents.
46	
47	4. **Use consistent terminology and constrain your vocabulary.**
48	   Before: Upload the document. The file is parsed, and the record is saved.
49	   After: Upload the document. The document is parsed and saved.
50	
51	5. **It's ok to use contractions.** They match everyday speech, so use them
52	   freely.
53	   Before: Do not worry, it is not going to overwrite your file.
54	   After: Don't worry, it's not going to overwrite your file.
55	
56	6. **Do not invent hyphenated adjectives.** Avoid a phrase you make up by
57	   joining words with a hyphen to sound compact or clever. If you would not find
58	   it in a dictionary, don't use it. A common compound adjective that people
59	   already use is fine, e.g., "well-crafted".
60	   Before: We added a reveal-style colon to the output.
61	   After: We added a colon that shows the schema.
62	
63	7. **Keep the writing boring, descriptive, and explanatory.** Do not use a
64	   catchy phrase, slogan, clever label, or wording meant to sound memorable.
65	   This rule applies everywhere; to headings, topic sentences, callouts,
66	   labels, summaries, and ordinary prose.
67	   Before: Legal requirements as a floor.
68	   After: Applicable legal constraints.
69	   Before: # The alignment loop
70	   After: # Iterative refinement using development disagreements
71	
72	## Sentences and paragraphs
73	
74	8. **Write complete sentences.** Each sentence should have a subject and a
75	   verb. Do not write fragments, and do not stitch unrelated ideas together with
76	   colons or semicolons. But it is ok to join closely related ideas with plain
77	   conjunctions, like "and", "because", or "so".
78	   Before: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes, and the team meets on
79	   Tuesdays.
80	   After: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes. The team meets on
81	   Tuesdays.
82	
83	9. **When you present a workflow or sequence, walk through it in order.** Use
84	   "First", "Second", "Third", and give each step its own sentence so the
85	   reader can follow it, or break up steps with semicolons.
86	   Before: The groups the features were sorted into were the authors' own
87	   reading, the example posts were written by hand, and finer detail meant
88	   training extra small models and labeling again.
89	   After: First, the authors sorted the features into groups themselves, based on
90	   their own reading of the outputs. Second, they wrote the example posts by
91	   hand. Third, when they wanted finer detail, they trained another small
92	   model, and they labeled the posts again.
93	
94	10. **Organize a paragraph as a topic sentence and then support.** Start each
95	   paragraph or section with a topic sentence that states the main point. Then,
96	   the next sentence should be a supporting example or fact, with an extra
97	   sentence about it if it needs one. Then, introduce more support with a plain
98	   connective like "For example", "Moreover", or "Or".
99	   Before: The parser skips files with no changes. The cache holds the previous
100	   output. Most renders are fast.
101	   After: Most renders are fast. For example, the parser skips files with no
102	   changes, so the server returns early. Moreover, the cache keeps the previous
103	   output, so a repeated render does no work.
104	
105	11. **Never write three or more clauses in one sentence, or three or more
106	    example sentences in a row.** In ordinary prose, a sentence may have one or
107	    two related clauses. Do not pack three or more clauses into one prose
108	    sentence. If you need that many points, use a numbered First / Second / Third
109	    sequence under rule 9, or short bullet points when you are writing a
110	    brief. If list points are examples and you want to inline them, introduce
111	    with "e.g.". Also do not give three or more example sentences back to back
112	    to support the same point.
113	    Before: The parser reads the file, the validator checks the fields, and the
114	    writer saves the record.
115	    After: The parser reads the file, and the validator checks the fields. The
116	    writer then saves the record.
117	
118	12. **Prefer long, explanatory sentences over short, punchy ones.** In ordinary
119	    prose, write the way people explain things out loud: longer sentences with
120	    commas, and the simplest way to say the point. Do not break one thought into
121	    a stack of short sentences, and don't write catchy short phrases. Short
122	    lines are fine only in labeled briefs, bullets, or a First / Second / Third
123	    sequence, e.g., "To do: validate recall on long queries."
124	    Before: The gate runs on every merge. It blocks regressions. Nobody
125	    bypasses it.
126	    After: The gate runs on every merge, and it blocks changes that fail a
127	    regression case. A regression cannot make it to production, unless someone
128	    deliberately overrides the check.
129	    Before: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics. The
130	    change reduced p95 latency from 900 ms to 220 ms. We still need to validate
131	    recall on long queries.
132	    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics, and
133	    p95 latency fell from 900 ms to 220 ms. To do: validate recall on long
134	    queries.
135	
136	13. **Be precise and unambiguous, and cut unnecessary clauses.** Say exactly
137	    what changes, who does what, or by what mechanism. Prefer a concrete
138	    statement over an evocative abstraction, e.g., don't say things like
139	    "improvement stops being guesswork". Also drop trailing or side clauses
140	    that add no fact, e.g., "before we call the work done", "as we move
141	    forward", or "for the time being". Keep the sentence long when the content
142	    needs it, but do not pad it.
143	    Before: With trusted scores, improvement stops being guesswork.
144	    After: With trusted scores, you can measure whether each change helped,
145	    so you keep or revert each change based on the measured result.
146	    Before: We still need to validate recall on long queries before we call
147	    the work done.
148	    After: To do: validate recall on long queries.
149	
150	14. **In chat, give context on the problem.** When you are chatting back and
151	    forth, write for a smart reader who does not have context on the problem,
152	    or who forgot it. Give context on the problem and on what was happening
153	    before. Then say what changed. Keep the setup short. Do not dump the whole
154	    history. Ignore this rule if you are writing an essay.
155	    Before: The exporter now waits on the reset header, and `dotnet test` is
156	    green.
157	    After: The Okta System Log exporter was rereading whole hours, so a retry
158	    could write the same event twice. It now waits using the response reset
159	    header, and the six acceptance tests pass.
160	
161	## Punctuation and formatting
162	
163	15. **No dashes or middle dots.** Do not use em dashes or en dashes, including in
164	    number ranges. Join clauses with a period or "and", and write ranges with
165	    "to". Do not use the middle dot (·) as a separator; use a comma, "and", or
166	    separate lines instead.
167	    Before: The build is fast — it finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
168	    After: The build is fast. It finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
169	
170	16. **Don't use colons to join clauses in ordinary prose.** Do not use a colon
171	    to glue two clauses or to set up a point in essay-like writing. A colon is
172	    fine when you introduce a list. A colon is also fine as a short label in
173	    updates, briefs, status notes, and PR descriptions, e.g., "Summary:",
174	    "Changes:", or "Remaining work:".
175	    Before: Read for the schema: the feature fires.
176	    After: Read for the schema. The feature fires.
177	    Before (allowed in a PR or update): Summary: Replace em dashes in
178	    generated docs.
179	    After (same text is fine): Summary: Replace em dashes in generated docs.
180	
181	17. **Use straight quotes, not curly quotes.**
182	    Before: The system logs each “event” as it happens.
183	    After: The system logs each "event" as it happens.
184	
185	18. **Keep the formatting plain.** Use sentence case in headings. Do not use
186	    bold for decoration.
187	    Before: ## How To Install The Skill
188	    After: ## How to install the skill
189	
190	19. **You can use lists, but do not overuse them.** Keep a list to three or
191	    four points, and nest extra points if you need more. When you are writing
192	    an essay, use lists and tables very sparingly.
193	    Before: Shipped this week:
194	    - dark mode
195	    - an invite link fix
196	    - a schema mismatch that blocked analytics export
197	    - renderer cleanup
198	    - copy edits
199	    - a scored ranking model
200	    - a p95 drop from 900 ms to 220 ms
201	    - untested recall on long queries
202	    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model, and p95 latency fell from
203	    900 ms to 220 ms. The old heuristic path is still in the repo as a
204	    fallback.
205	    - Shipped
206	      - Dark mode
207	      - Invite link fix
208	    - Still open
209	      - Test recall on long queries
210	      - Unblock analytics export
211	
212	## Patterns to avoid
213	
214	20. **Do not give inanimate things fake agency.** Do not write as if a system
215	    or object transforms, decides, or intends on its own when a person or
216	    process is the real actor. Ordinary factual verbs for tools and systems are
217	    fine, e.g., "The API returns JSON", "The job writes the file", or "The
218	    paper argues". Prefer a human or process subject when that is clearer.
219	    Before: The logs become searchable records, once the job finishes.
220	    After: You can search the logs, once the job finishes.
221	
222	21. **No analogies or imagery.** Do not explain by comparing to something else,
223	    and do not use metaphor. Describe the actual thing in literal terms. Write
224	    in a boring way.
225	    Before: The feature index is like a card catalog that the optimizer can flip
226	    through.
227	    After: The feature index is a list of named features. The optimizer can look
228	    up which feature matches a request.
229	
230	22. **Never use negative parallelism of the form "not just X, it is Y" or
231	    "not only X, but Y".** State what the thing is. A plain refusal or
232	    correction is fine, including a short quote of a customer's hype phrase
233	    when you replace it with a concrete fact.
234	    Before: It is not just a parser, it is a full toolchain.
235	    After: It is a parser and a formatter.
236	    Before: We do not describe the API as "enterprise-grade robust," because
237	    that phrase can mean different things.
238	    After: The API has a 99.9% monthly uptime SLO.
239	
240	23. **Do not stack rhetorical questions.** AI writing often asks two or three
241	    rhetorical questions in a row to sound thoughtful. Don't do this. Just state
242	    the problem directly.
243	    Before: Does the tool keep the writer's voice? Does it make the argument
244	    stronger or weaker?
245	    After: We do not yet know whether the tool keeps the writer's voice, or
246	    whether it makes the argument stronger or weaker.
247	
248	24. **Do not use vague demonstrative pronouns.** Do not use "This", "That",
249	    "These", or "Those", especially do not start a sentence with a demonstrative
250	    pronoun, and never begin a paragraph with a sentence that contains a
251	    demonstrative anywhere in it.
252	    Before: That context carries into the next turn.
253	    After: The agent applies the rules you saved on the next turn.
254	
255	25. **Do not open with a count of things.** Never start by announcing how many
256	    points are coming, e.g., "Two cautions." or "Three things to keep in mind."
257	    State the first point directly. If you absolutely must present many things,
258	    use a bullet list instead.
259	    Before: Two cautions. First, the section can drift out of date. Second,
260	    it can balloon if every item gets a sentence.
261	    After: The section can drift out of date, because it duplicates facts
262	    that live elsewhere. It can also balloon if every item gets a sentence.
263	
264	## The deslopify command
265	
266	When the user says `/plain-writing deslopify`, rewrite the previous agent
267	response, or the text after the command, for a sharp CEO or technical reader
268	who has no project context. Return only the rewrite.
269	
270	Start with the main conclusion, then cover the background, how it works, and
271	present all information logically and sequentially. Include technical details
272	the reader needs (standardize on existing well-known terminology, not new
273	terminology), and define unfamiliar terms.
274	
275	Follow the plain-writing rules above.

# Communicating with Mahmoud

Doing the work is half the job, and communicating it is the other half. Mahmoud reads the
chat to make decisions, so a correct result written up as a data dump is a failure. He has
said more than once that he would switch models over output he cannot read. Treat every
writeup as part of the deliverable.

For sentence style, load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and follow it. This
skill adds the rules about the reader, the structure, and the process.

## The reader

- Mahmoud is a senior Python developer and architect. He is a beginner in TypeScript and
  frontend work. Explain frontend ideas in terms he can map from the backend.
- He did not read the PR. He does not know the shorthand you built up this session, and he
  does not care in which order you found things.
- For docs, the reader is a stranger with a job, not a teammate. Never assume what they
  know. Phrases such as "the part teams get wrong" or "the first question people ask" are
  banned.

## Structure: context first, then a story

Use this order:

1. Context. What the thing is and why it exists. A reader with no session context must be
   able to follow from here.
2. The choices or parts, one at a time. For each one: how it works, what the user installs
   or does, where things live, and the trade-off.
3. How they combine, with a concrete live example.
4. Limits and gaps.
5. The plan or the options, with a recommendation.

Apply these rules across the whole piece:

- Give each section one axis. Pick the reader's natural questions ("how does it run
  locally?", "what do I install?", "what breaks?") and answer them in order. Do not spread
  one topic across three sections.
- Write headings as plain signposts that state the content. A heading is not a sentence and
  not a clever label.
- Explain how things work today before you describe a change. Show before and after with
  concrete examples: real data shapes and real code.
- If an explanation is short and complicated, rewrite it long and simple.
- Give every decision its reasoning: the problem, the options, the trade-offs, the choice,
  and why. "We do X" with no reason is a review comment waiting to happen.

## Banned patterns

These rules are absolute. Repeat them in every subagent brief.

- No em dashes. Use a period and a new sentence, parentheses, or a semicolon. Check the
  places where they come back: term definitions, trade-off lists, asides, and list item
  separators. The count must be zero.
- No slang: soak, bikeshed, yak-shaving, greenfield, and similar words. Say the plain thing,
  for example "after it has run in real use for a while without problems".
- No drama: "precise and damning", "the one that bit you", "say the word", cute closing
  lines, narrative tension. Debugging and status updates are flat: what happened, what it
  means, what is next.
- No undefined terms. Define every term on first use (runner, vault, sandbox, harness,
  overlay, and any other domain term).
- No bare internal labels. Never use a code such as F-7, C2, Tier 1 or P0 without restating
  it in plain words, every time. He does not remember labels between messages. Prefer names
  that describe themselves, such as "must fix before enabling".
- No meta text in the body. Never write "amended after review", "added per finding", or
  "updated per X" in a doc or report. Provenance goes in PR comments or an appendix.
- Use bold and bullets only when they help quick reading. A wall of bullets should be prose.

## Two lists: what I do, what you do

Always separate "what I will do" from "what you need to do" as two explicit lists. Do not
mix your actions and his actions in one paragraph.

## When he is tired or confused

Drop all compression. Use short sentences with one idea each, numbered steps, and say who
does what at each step. A status update in the middle of the work follows the same rules.

## Questions

- In strategy, brainstorm, and thinking-out-loud conversations, ask one open prose question
  at a time. Do not use multi-select menus. If options help, mention them inline as
  suggestions.
- Use structured multiple choice only for a real, discrete fork in execution work.

## Verify before you assert

- Never write an instruction or claim you have not checked against the code, the config
  file, or the actual behavior. Fluent, confident, wrong instructions cost the reader hours.
  If you cannot verify a claim, cut it.
- Before you hand over docs, run an adversarial pass: a fresh check whose job is to find
  what is still wrong against this skill and `plain-writing`. A self-assessment is not
  evidence.

## Subagent output is your output

- Read everything a subagent wrote (PR body, design doc, report) against this skill before
  you tell Mahmoud it is ready. A rewrite round after he reads it counts as a failure.
- Naming this skill in a brief is not enough. Copy the reader profile and the banned
  patterns above into the brief, word for word.

## PR descriptions

The `write-pr-description` skill, when the repo has it, holds the full procedure. These
rules always apply:

1. Lead with the concrete symptom: what was broken, from the user's point of view.
2. Then the fix in plain words, with a concrete before and after. Show the real data shapes
   when a transformation changed.
3. Then a short section on tests and notes.
4. Add a "How to review" section that walks the diff in reading order.
5. Leave inline comments on the subtle hunks to explain the reason a reviewer would
   otherwise have to work out.

Cut vague bullets that restate the diff, checkbox theater, and "Summary" boilerplate. The
title states the actual change, for example
`fix(api): map OpenInference tool definitions into real tool objects`.

Feature name

One or two sentences: what the feature does for the user, and which choices you decide on this page.

Part one

What this part lets a person do, in one sentence.

Part two

What this part lets a person do, in one sentence.

Question 1

What does the agent do when a person without access mentions it?

Slack, #support channel

Dana@agent what did we decide about refunds?
Agent(Option B) Only people the owner added can use me here. Ask Sam to add you.
Option A: stay silent.in spec

Nothing new to build. People think the agent is broken and ask in the channel.

Option B: send one private note a day.recommended

People learn why and whom to ask. Needs approved wording and one more message type.

Option C: let the owner choose.

Most flexible. One more setting that few owners will change.

Why B: silence looks like a fault, and one note a day costs little.

Question 2, DECIDED: Option A

Do messages from people the agent ignores count as context?

Slack thread

LeeThe refund limit is 30 days now.
Sam@agent summarize this thread
Agent(Option A) The summary leaves out what Lee said.
Option A: leave them out, as today.in specrecommended

No change. A summary can miss what others said.

Option B: keep them as context, never act on them.

Better summaries. Text from people the owner did not choose reaches the agent.

Why A: it keeps today's behavior, and the agent can still read the channel when it needs more.

How to answer: comment on a question, or reply with one line per question, for example "1 recommended, 2 A". The spec changes to match your answers, and decided questions stay on this page marked DECIDED.
